title: Strings
summary: Store text, read individual characters, and build new **strings**.
refresher: `std::string` stores text. **Indexes** begin at zero, `.size()` gives the character count, and `+` joins compatible **strings**. Include `<string>` before using this type.

blocks.body: Use `std::string` for words and sentences. Include `<string>`, then create a **value** such as `std::string name = "Ada";`. A single `char` stores only one character, while a **string** stores many.

**String** positions start at zero. In `"code"`, **index** zero is `c` and index three is `e`. `.size()` returns the number of characters, so the final valid index is one less than the size. Check that a string is not empty before asking for its last character.

blocks.title: Strings feel familiar from Python
blocks.body: Python and C++ **strings** both start indexing at zero. Python writes `len(word)`, while C++ writes `word.size()`. C++ also places the type in the `std` library namespace, which is why its full name is `std::string`.

blocks.caption: The first bracket reads the first character. substr starts at **index** one and takes three characters.
Check that text exists before reading its final character.
blocks.wrong: char last = text[text.size() - 1]; // unsafe when empty

blocks.body: For a nonempty word, `back()` returns the final character. An empty **string** has no final character, so the `if` **condition** skips that access. Remember that a size is a count, not a position.

blocks.title: The size is one past the last index
blocks.body: A four-character **string** has a size of four but valid **indexes** from zero through three. `text[text.size()]` goes one position beyond the string.

blocks.why: The **string** contains three characters, so its size is three.
The call starts at **index** one and takes two characters, producing od.

blocks.title: Strings checklist
items: Check emptiness before using the last character.

strings-lesson-check-1.title: Length is not the last index
strings-lesson-check-1.body: String positions start at 0, so the count is one past the final valid index.
strings-lesson-check-1.notice: A five-character string uses positions 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4.
strings-lesson-check-1.mistake: Do not use the length itself as an index unless you mean one past the end.

strings-lesson-check-2.title: Follow each string operation
strings-lesson-check-2.body: When several string methods appear together, trace the returned value from left to right before choosing the output.
strings-lesson-check-2.notice: Some methods return strings, and some return collections of smaller pieces.
strings-lesson-check-2.mistake: Do not keep measuring the original text after a method has returned a different value.

strings-summary-01.title: Strings are text values
strings-summary-01.body: A **string** stores text. You can measure it, read characters by position, take pieces from it, and build new text from it.
strings-summary-01.notice: Most string operations return a value; they do not rewrite the original text in place.
strings-summary-01.mistake: Do not treat the character count as the final valid position.

strings-supplement-01.title: Strings do not change in place
strings-supplement-01.body: Many beginner bugs come from trying to edit one character inside a string. Instead, build a new string with the change you want.
strings-supplement-01.notice: Immutable means the original text value is not edited directly.
strings-supplement-01.mistake: Do not assign into a string index like it is a list slot.

strings-authored-01.title: Convert before joining text and numbers
strings-authored-01.body: Joining text with a number needs an explicit conversion or a formatted string. That makes the intended output clear.
strings-authored-01.notice: The plus operator can mean different things depending on the values around it.
strings-authored-01.mistake: Do not expect the language to always guess whether plus means addition or text joining.

strings-authored-02.title: Index errors come from bounds
strings-authored-02.body: If code asks for a string position that does not exist, the bug is usually a zero-based counting mistake.
strings-authored-02.notice: Check both the string length and the position being requested.
strings-authored-02.mistake: Do not read the final character before checking that the string is nonempty.

strings-authored-03.title: Use the method result
strings-authored-03.body: A string method call often gives back transformed text. Store, return, print, or compare that returned value.
strings-authored-03.notice: Calling the method alone may do nothing visible.
strings-authored-03.mistake: Do not assume a string method changed the variable automatically.

strings-authored-04.title: Reach the final character safely
strings-authored-04.body: To read the last character, use the language's last-index pattern and first make sure the string has at least one character.
strings-authored-04.notice: Last-index shortcuts are convenient, but empty strings still have no last character.
strings-authored-04.mistake: Do not use the count as the final index.

strings-authored-05.title: Slices stop before the end
strings-authored-05.body: A slice or substring range usually includes the start and stops before the ending position.
strings-authored-05.notice: The stop value acts like a boundary, not a character to include.
strings-authored-05.mistake: Do not count the stop position as part of the returned text.

strings-authored-06.title: Normalize typed text before comparing
strings-authored-06.body: When people type answers, spaces and capitalization can vary. Clean the text before comparing when exact formatting is not the point.
strings-authored-06.notice: Normalize both the value and the comparison target in the same way.
strings-authored-06.mistake: Do not clean only one side of a comparison and leave the other side inconsistent.
